Content: An object is moving to the right with speed `v_i` when a force of magnitude `F` is exerted on it. In which of the following situations is the object's direction of motion changing and kinetic energy decreasing at the instant shown?

Key.Rationale: A force exerted perpendicular to the direction of motion changes the direction of the object's motion but does not change the object's speed.

force directed “backwards” compared to the object's motion - in this case a leftward force exerted on an object moving to the right - slows down the object but does not change its direction of motion.

The object does indeed change direction, because the force is not parallel or antiparallel to the direction of motion, but a component of the force points in the direction of motion (rightward), making the object speed up, not slow down.

Break the force direction into components parallel and perpendicular to the object's motion. The leftward parallel component points backwards compared to the velocity, so the object slows down. And the perpendicular (up-the-page) component changes the object's direction of motion.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/2a.jpg

A ball is suspended by a lightweight string, as shown in the figure above. The ball is displaced to position `1` and released. The `text(four)` labeled positions are evenly spaced along the arc of the ball's motion. Between which adjacent pairs of positions is the change in kinetic energy of the ball greatest?

Key.Rationale: Mechanical energy stays constant during the ball's swing. During `text(each segment)`, the kinetic energy gained by the ball equals the gravitational potential energy lost by the `text(ball/Earth)` system. Between `1` and `2`, the ball loses the most height, and hence, the system loses the most gravitational potential energy (`DeltaU_text(grave)=mgDeltay`).

Although the ball travels the same distance from `2` to `3` as it traveled from `1` to `2`, the ball “falls” through less vertical distance between `2` and `3`. The system loses less gravitational potential energy between `2` and `3` than it did between `1` and `2`, and therefore gains less kinetic energy.

The ball loses much less height (vertical distance) between `3` and `4` than it did between `1` and `2`. Therefore it loses less potential energy - and gains less kinetic energy - between `3` and `4`.

D.Choice: The change is the same for all adjacent pairs.

Key.Rationale: During `text(each successive segment)`, the ball loses less height and hence the system loses less gravitational potential energy. Therefore, over `text(each successive segment)`, the ball gains less kinetic energy.

Content: A newly discovered planet is found to have density `2/3rho_E` and radius `2R_E` , where `rho_E` and `R_E` are the density and radius of `text(Earth)`, respectively. The surface gravitational field of the planet is most nearly

Key.Rationale: This would be correct if the new planet's mass were `text(two-thirds)` of the `text(Earth's)` mass and its radius were `text(twice)` the Earth's. But because the new planet has `text(twice)` the `text(Earth's)` radius, its volume is `text(eight)` times larger than `text(Earth's)`. “Filling” that larger volume results in a planet more massive than `text(Earth)`, though less dense.

Other things being equal, `text(doubling)` the radius of the planet would reduce the gravitational field at its surface by a factor of `4`, not a factor of `2`. `text(Doubling)` its radius also increases its mass, as explained in the correct choice.

If the new planet differed from `text(Earth)` only in having `text(two-thirds)` the density, then its mass would be `text(two-thirds)` of `text(Earth's)` and hence its gravitational field would be `text(two-thirds)` of `text(Earth's)`, about `6.7` `text(m)//text(s)^2`. But the new planet is also bigger than `text(Earth)`.

Other things being equal, `text(doubling)` a planet's radius would cut the gravitational field to `text(one-fourth)`, due to the `text(square)` in `g=F_text(grave)//m=GM//r^2`. But the new planet also has more mass than `text(Earth)`. `text(Doubling)` the radius increases the volume by a factor of `8`; but this does not mean the mass increases by `8` times, because the planet's density is `text(two-thirds)` that of `text(Earth)`. Instead, the new planet's mass is `text(two-thirds)` of `8` times the `text(Earth's)`, i.e., `2//3**8=5.3`. times the mass of `text(Earth)`. Taking both mass and radius into account, the new planet's `g` is `(5.3)//4` times the `text(Earth's)`: `9.8` `text(m)//text(s)^2**(5.3)//4=13` `text(N)//text(kg)`.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/4a.jpg

A bus is initially traveling north at a constant speed, as shown in the figure above. As the bus starts to make a left turn without changing speed, a passenger notices that a box on the floor starts sliding toward the right side of the bus. Which of the following top views of the box, when correctly labeled, would best represent all of the horizontal forces exerted on the box as it starts sliding?

Key.Rationale: The box slides to the right with respect to the bus, but not because a rightward (eastward) force is exerted on the box. The box's inertia is what leads it to slide rightward with respect to the bus: Because the bus starts gaining westward velocity while the box's velocity initially keeps it moving purely northward, the bus is moving westward relative to the box. Therefore, the box is moving eastward (to the right) relative to the bus.
While the box slides rightward relative to the bus, the floor of the bus exerts a frictional force that opposes the box's motion - a force directed to the left.
The box initially retains its northward velocity, but not force acts on it. `text(Once)` it is already moving northward, the box's inertia keeps it moving northward (Newton's `1^text(st)` law).
No rightward force is exerted on the box.

Content: Which block takes the longest time to reach the ground?

Key.Rationale: Because no force opposes the gravitational force exerted on the block, it has the “full” free-fall acceleration of `9 8` `text(m)//text(s)^2` and it also has the shortest distance to travel.

Block `B` arrives at the ground with just as much speed as block `A`. But block `B` takes more time to reach the ground, for `text(two)` reasons. `text(First)`, `B` covers more distance than `A`. `text(Second)`, `B` has a smaller acceleration, because the normal force exerted by the ramp partially opposes the downward force exerted by gravity on `B`.

Block `C` lands just as quickly as block `A`. Although `C` covers more total distance, both blocks start with the same vertical velocity (`v_(0y)=0`) and cover the same vertical distance (`Deltay=h`) with the same vertical acceleration (`a_y=g`). Therefore, they take the same time. The horizontal motion of `C` has no effect on its vertical motion.

D.Choice: The blocks take the same time to reach the ground.

Key.Rationale: `A` and `C` land at the same time, but `B` takes more time to reach the ground.

Content: Which block has the greatest speed just before hitting the ground?

Key.Rationale: Because blocks `A` and `C` start with the same vertical velocity (`v_(0y)=0`) and fall through the same vertical distance (`Deltay=h`) with the same vertical acceleration (`a_y=g`), they end up with the same vertical velocity. But block `C`, unlike block `A`, has horizontal velocity as well. So, block `A` ends up with less overall speed (just before hitting the ground).

Blocks `A` and `B` reach the ground with the same kinetic energy and hence the same speed. This is because they both start at rest, and both `text(block-Earth)` systems lose the same potential energy (`DeltaU_text(grav)=-mgh`) and hence gain the same kinetic energy.

In all `text(three)` cases, the same potential energy is lost and hence the same kinetic energy is gained. But block `C`, unlike `A` and `B`, starts with `text(nonzero)` kinetic energy. This initial kinetic energy adds onto the kinetic energy it gains, giving `C` the biggest final kinetic energy and therefore the most speed.

D.Choice: The blocks reach the ground with the same speed.

Key.Rationale: Although all `text(three)` blocks gain the same kinetic energy, block `C` starts with the most kinetic energy and therefore ends up with the greatest kinetic energy (and therefore speed).

Content: A ball is dropped from rest and falls to the floor. The initial gravitational potential energy of the `text(ball-Earth-floor)` system is `10` `text(J)`. The ball then bounces back up to a height where the gravitational potential energy is `7` `text(J)`. What was the mechanical energy of the `text(ball-Earth-floor)` system the instant the ball left the floor?

Key.Rationale: The system's potential energy is `text(zero)` at that point (if we set `y=0` at the floor). But the ball is moving upward and therefore has `text(nonzero)` kinetic energy. Therefore, its mechanical energy (`K+U`) is `text(nonzero)`.
The system loses `3` `text(J)` of mechanical energy during the bounce; but that's different from how much mechanical energy the system still has after it bounces.

After the ball leaves the floor, the system no longer gains or loses mechanical energy as the ball rises to its peak. As it rises, kinetic energy converts to gravitational potential energy, but the mechanical energy (`K+U`) stays the same. As a result, the system has the same mechanical energy immediately after the bounce as it has at the peak.

The system's mechanical energy changes from `10` `text(J)` to `7` `text(J)` during the bounce, when some mechanical energy dissipates largely as thermal energy. No mechanical energy dissipates while the ball rises.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/8a.jpg

A disk is initially rotating counterclockwise around a fixed axis with angular speed `omega_0`. At time `t=0`, the `text(two)` forces shown in the figure above are exerted on the disk. If counterclockwise is positive, which of the following could show the angular velocity of the disk as a function of time?

Key.Rationale: Because the question defines counterclockwise as positive, the disk's initial angular velocity is positive; however graph `A` shows the initial angular velocity as negative.
Because the torques exerted on the disk do not balance, the disk changes angular velocity; however graph `B` shows the angular velocity as constant.

The net torque on the disk is constant and oriented clockwise. So, the disk has a constant clockwise angular acceleration. Because counterclockwise is positive, this angular acceleration - the rate of change of the angular velocity - is constant and negative.

It correctly shows the disk's angular speed as its counterclockwise angular velocity steadily decreases to `text(zero)` and then its clockwise angular velocity steadily increases. The angular velocity graph should depict the clockwise and counterclockwise angular velocities as having opposite signs.

Content: A `50.0` `text(N)` box is at rest on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the surface is `0.50`, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is `0.30`. A horizontal `20.0` `text(N)` force is then exerted on the box. The magnitude of the acceleration of the box is most nearly

Key.Rationale: The maximum force of static friction that the floor can exert on the box is `mu_sF_text(normal)=mu_sF_text(grav)=(0.50)(50.0` `text(N))=25` `text(N)`. Therefore, the `20.0` `text(N)` horizontal force exerted on the box cannot overcome the static frictional force, and the box remains at rest.
The `0.50` coefficient of static friction does not necessarily equal the box's acceleration.

If the box were moving, the frictional force exerted on it would be `(0.30)F_text(normal)=15` `text(N)`, and hence the net horizontal force would be `20` `text(N)-15` `text(N)=5` `text(N)`, causing an acceleration of about `1` `text(m)//text(s)^2`. However, the force of static friction prevents the block from moving.

If no frictional force were exerted on the block, then the net force would be `20.0` `text(N)`, causing the box to accelerate at about `4` `text(m)//text(s)^2`. But the net horizontal force includes a frictional force.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/10a.jpg

A thin rod of length d on a frictionless surface is pivoted about `text(one)` end, as shown above, and can rotate freely. The rod is at rest when it is struck by a sphere with linear momentum of magnitude `p_i` perpendicular to the rod. The sphere rebounds along its original line of motion with momentum of magnitude `p_f`. What is the magnitude of the angular momentum of the rod immediately after the collision?

Key.Rationale: If the given initial momentum were expressed as a negative number, then `p_f-p_i` would give the sphere's change in linear momentum. However the sphere's change in linear momentum cannot be equated to the rod's change in angular momentum.

`p_f+p_i` is the ball's change in linear momentum. This cannot be equated to the rod's change in angular momentum, because linear and angular momenta are different physical quantities (as indicated by their different units).

If the given initial momentum were expressed as a negative number, then this would be the magnitude of the sphere's - and hence the rod's - change in angular momentum. But the given linear momenta are both magnitudes.

Because `p=mv`, pd is just another way of expressing `mvr`, the sphere's angular momentum with respect to the rod's pivot. Therefore, `(p_f+p_i)d` is the sphere's change in angular momentum. The terms are added because the sphere's overall change in angular momentum is the lost counterclockwise angular momentum (`p_i d`) plus the gained clockwise momentum (`p_fd`). Because angular momentum stays constant during the collision, the rod's angular momentum changes by the same amount.

Content: A spacecraft is placed in a circular orbit around a planet with mass `6.4xx10^23` `text(kg)`. The spacecraft orbits at a height of `4.5xx10^7` `text(m)` above the planet's surface. What additional information is needed to calculate the speed of the spacecraft in the orbit?

Key.Rationale: The distance of the spacecraft from the center of the planet is needed, but only the altitude above the surface is given.

Orbital velocity is found by equating gravitational force from Newton's law of gravitation with the product of spacecraft mass and centripetal acceleration, and solving for velocity. The result depends only on `G`, planet mass and distance from the center of the planet. Because height above the surface is given, the planet radius is also needed to find the orbit radius.
Because gravitational mass and inertial mass are equal, the spacecraft mass cancels in the solution.

D.Choice: Both the planet's radius and the spacecraft's mass

Key.Rationale: The planet's radius is needed to calculate the orbit radius, but the spacecraft mass will cancel.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/12a.jpg

`text(Two)` carts, of mass `2m` and `m`, approach each other head-on with the same speed `v`, as shown in the figure above. When the carts collide, they hook together. Assuming positive momentum is to the right, which of the following best represents the momentum of the cart of mass `m` as a function of time before and after the collision?

Key.Rationale: It shows a constant negative momentum for the cart of mass `m` before and after the collision. Momentum conservation of a system can be misinterpreted to mean that momentum of an object is always the same.

It has the correct relative magnitudes of the momentum of the cart of mass `m` before and after the collision but the cart still moving to the left. The “backward” change in momentum of the cart could be confused with a negative sign for direction

By momentum conservation, `2mv-mv=mv=(3m)(v//3)`, so carts after collision move with speed `v//3` to the right. Thus momentum of the cart of mass `m` before collision is `-mv` and after collision is `+mv//3` as shown in the graph for this option.
It assumes that the cart of mass `m` would move at speed `v` to the right after the collision. The final system momentum could be confused with the final momentum of block `m`.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/13a.jpg

A student stands at `text(one)` end of a raft floating in a pool with equally spaced marks along the bottom, as shown above. The student and the raft have the same mass. The student walks to the opposite end of the raft. Which of the following best shows the final locations of the raft and student relative to the marks at the bottom of the pool? Assume that there is no drag force between the raft and the water.

Key.Rationale: It shows the motion of the student across the raft driving both the raft and student forward.
It shows the raft remaining at rest while the student walks along it.

Because the mass of the student and the mass of the raft are the same, the system center of mass must be `text(halfway)` between the object centers, i.e., at `2.5` divisions from the left edge of the pool. With no external forces the position of the center of mass remains unchanged, so when the student reaches the other end of the raft the new point `text(halfway)` between the student and the center of the raft must once again be at `2.5` divisions from the left edge of the pool.

It assumes that there is no force between the raft and water, which would result in the student walking over the surface of the raft without moving relative to the pool, and the raft being pushed backward.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/14a.jpg

A circuit is designed with `text(two)` resistors, `R_1=200` `Omega` and `R_2=400` `Omega`, and a battery with internal resistance `R=10` `Omega`, as shown above. What is the relationship between the `text(three)` labeled currents?

Key.Rationale: It assumes that the current through the battery is split between the resistors in the circuit independent of circuit arrangement.
It assumes that the current through a smaller resistance is larger than that through a larger resistance independent of the circuit arrangement.
It assumes that the current is larger through a larger resistance independent of the circuit arrangement.

Because all `text(three)` resistors are connected in series, conservation of charge (Kirchoff 's junction rule) requires that the rate of charge transport through all the circuit elements must be the same.

Content: When `text(two)` charged, massive objects are placed a distance `r` apart, the gravitational force between them has magnitude `F`. When the distance between the objects is increased to `2r`, the magnitude of the gravitational force between them becomes `F//4` . Did the electrostatic force between the objects also decrease to `text(one fourth)` its initial magnitude as a result of the change in position, and why?

A.Choice: No, because the gravitational constant is much smaller than the electrostatic constant.

Key.Rationale: Although the value of the constants is very different, the value has no effect on the behavior of the forces with changing separation between the objects as long as the charges and masses are unchanged.

B.Choice: No, because the gravitational force is only attractive, and the electrostatic force can also be repulsive.

Key.Rationale: Although the gravitational force is only attractive, this has no effect on the behavior of the forces as the separation between the objects is changed.

C.Choice: Yes, because both forces have the same `1//r^2` dependence.

Key.Rationale: Both forces have an inverse square dependence. With mass and charge unchanged, the only factor affecting the forces is the change in separation, and each is reduced to `1/4` of its original value by doubling

D.Choice: Yes, because the gravitational force always equals the electrostatic force at any given distance.

Key.Rationale: Although the electrostatic force will decrease to `text(one fourth)` of its value, the magnitude of the `text(two)` forces depends on the masses of the objects and the net charges on the objects. If those remain unchanged, it is the ratio of the magnitudes of the `text(two)` forces that will be the same at any given distance.

Content: Cart `A` moves horizontally on a frictionless track. It collides and sticks to identical cart `B`, which is at rest. The speed of cart `A` before the collision is measured to be `3.0` `text(m)//text(s)`, with an uncertainty of `+-0.2` `text(m)//text(s)`. Students are asked to predict the speed of the carts after the collision. Given the uncertainty of the measurement for the speed of cart `A`, which of the following is the best prediction?

Key.Rationale: It is obtained by taking `text(half)` of `3 0` `text(m)//text(s)`, applying an uncertainty of `+-0.2` `text(m)//text(s)` as in the correct option, and then applying an additional uncertainty of `+-0.2` `text(m)//text(s)` to the range obtained for the correct option. It is a prediction of the range of measured values of the speed assuming that the predicted range in the correct option is correct.

It is not a prediction of the actual range of the speed after the collision given the uncertainty of the initial speed, but of the range of measurements of that speed assuming the same measuring process is used.
It is obtained by taking `text(half)` of `3 0` `text(m)//text(s)` and creating a range by applying an uncertainty of `+-0.2` `text(m)//text(s)`.

For this inelastic collision, the value of the speed after the collision will be `text(half)` of the speed of cart `A` before the collision. The speed of cart `A` could be anywhere from `2.8` `text(m)//text(s)` up to `3.2` `text(m)//text(s)`, so the predicted speed would be between `1.4` `text(m)//text(s)` and `1.6` `text(m)//text(s)`. This is not a prediction of the range of measured speeds after the collision, which would depend on the precision of the measuring process used.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/17a.jpg

A lion is running at constant speed toward a gazelle that is standing still, as shown in the top figure above. After several `text(seconds)`, the gazelle notices the lion and accelerates directly toward him, hoping to pass the lion and force him to reverse direction. As the gazelle accelerates toward and past the lion, the lion changes direction and accelerates in pursuit of the gazelle. The lion and the gazelle eventually each reach constant but different speeds. Which of the following sets of graphs shows a reasonable representation of the velocities of the lion and the gazelle as functions of time?

Key.Rationale: The graph for the lion shows an initial velocity toward the left, slowing down to `text(zero)`, and speeding up to the right and reaching a constant velocity to the right. The graph for the gazelle shows the gazelle initially at rest for a period of time, then speeding up to the right, and reaching a constant velocity toward the right
The graph for the lion matches the description, but the graph for the gazelle has the gazelle immediately speeding up to the right, rather than being at rest for several `text(seconds)`.

The graph for the lion shows the lion moving slowly to the right at `text(first)` and then speeding up to the right. The graph for the gazelle shows the gazelle speeding up from the start. Neither graph matches the story.
The graph for the gazelle is correct, but the graph for the lion is incorrect for the reason given in the correct option.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/18a.jpg

A spacecraft of mass `4000` `text(kg)` is traveling in a straight line in the positive direction. Engines can be fired so that the force exerted on the spacecraft is in the positive or negative direction. The graph above shows data for the force during `text(one)` interval. Which of the following is the best estimate of the net change in the speed of the spacecraft from time `t=0` to time `t=4` `text(s)`?

Key.Rationale: The answer is obtained by calculating the area of the `text(two)` sections under the force-time graph as positive.

The change in speed is given by the impulse divided by the mass. The impulse can be found by calculating the area under the force-time graph in `text(two)` sections. The `text(first)` is a positive area of the triangle between `text(zero)` and `2` `text(s)`, and the `text(second)` is the negative area of a rectangle between `3` and `4` `text(s)`.
The answer is obtained by calculating the area under the force-time graph with the triangular section as negative and the rectangular section as positive.
The answer is obtained by calculating the area of the `text(two)` sections under the force-time graph as negative.

Content: A rocket is continuously firing its engines as it accelerates away from `text(Earth)`. For the `text(first kilometer)` of its ascent, the mass of fuel ejected is small compared to the mass of the rocket. For this distance, which of the following indicates the changes, if any, in the kinetic energy of the rocket, the gravitational potential energy of the `text(Earth-rocket)` system, and the mechanical energy of the `text(Earth-rocket)` system?

A.Choice:
Rocket Kinetic `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Gravitational Potential `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Mechanical `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing

Key.Rationale: The rocket's velocity will increase with a negligible decrease in mass resulting in an increase in the rocket's kinetic energy. The gravitational potential energy is proportional to `-1//r` resulting in an increase in potential energy as `r` increases. The `text(Earth-rocket)` system's energy resulting from the addition of the rocket's kinetic energy and the system's potential energy will also increase.

B.Choice:
Rocket Kinetic `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Gravitational Potential `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Mechanical `ultext(Energy)`: Constant

Key.Rationale: The `text(Earth-rocket)` system's energy is composed of the kinetic energy of the rocket and the gravitational potential energy between them. If they both increase, the system's mechanical energy must increase as well. Work is being done on the system by the fuel so the system's energy is not constant.

C.Choice:
Rocket Kinetic `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Gravitational Potential `ultext(Energy)`: Decreasing
System Mechanical `ultext(Energy)`: Decreasing

Key.Rationale: As r increases, the system's gravitational potential energy must increase as it is proportional to `-1//r`. Consequently the system's mechanical energy does not decrease either.

D.Choice:
Rocket Kinetic `ultext(Energy)`: Decreasing
System Gravitational Potential `ultext(Energy)`: Increasing
System Mechanical `ultext(Energy)`: Constant

Key.Rationale: The rocket speeds up as it accelerates away from `text(Earth)`. The decrease in rocket mass is negligible therefore the kinetic energy must increase, not decrease. The change in kinetic energy should yield a change in the system's mechanical energy which does not remain constant.

Content: Block `1` is attached to a spring and oscillates on a horizontal frictionless surface. When block `1` is at a point of maximum displacement, block `2` is placed on top of it from directly above without interrupting the oscillation, and the `text(two)` blocks stick together. How do the maximum kinetic energy and period of oscillation with both blocks compare to those of block `1` alone?

Key.Rationale: The addition of block `2` does not affect the maximum kinetic energy because it is equal to the maximum spring potential energy. The period of oscillation is given by `2pisqrt(m/k)` therefore by increasing the mass of the oscillating object the period will increase.
The maximum kinetic energy is equal to the maximum spring potential energy which has not changed due to the addition of a block because it was placed while at maximum displacement.
The period of oscillation is given by `2pisqrt(m/k)`. By increasing the mass of the oscillating object, the period will increase.

The maximum kinetic energy is equal to the maximum spring potential energy `1/2kx^2` which has not changed because of the addition of a block because it was placed while at maximum displacement. The period of oscillation is given by `2pisqrt(m/k)`so increasing the mass of the oscillating object, the period will increase.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/21a.jpg
problems/AP14P1/media/21b.jpg

A child slides from rest down slides `A` and `B` shown above. The slides are the same height, and the coefficient of friction between the slides and the child is the same. Which of the following compares the change `DeltaK` in the kinetic energy of the child and the change `DeltaU` in the potential energy of the `text(child-Earth)` system for the `text(two)` slides?

Key.Rationale: There is friction between the child and slide and so the work done by friction is greater with slide `B` where the displacement is larger. Therefore slide `B` will leave the child with a smaller amount of kinetic energy than slide `A`.
The change in height of both slides is the same, leading to equal changes in potential energy for the system.

There is friction between the child and the slides, which is greater for slide `B` since the normal force is greater there. The displacement is also larger for slide `B` so it does more negative work. Therefore slide `B` will leave the child with a smaller amount of kinetic energy than slide `A`. The change in height of both slides is the same, leading to equal changes in potential energy for the system.
The change in height of both slides is the same, leading to equal changes in potential energy for the system.

Content: The student wishes to determine the spring constant of the spring using the measurements of the period of oscillation. Which of the following pieces of equipment would provide another measured quantity that is sufficient information to complete the determination of the spring constant?

Key.Rationale: There are no length measurements in the calculation of the spring constant because the equation for the period of oscillation is given by `2pisqrt(m/k)`.

The motion sensor would be redundant because the period has already been measured with a stopwatch. It would also neglect to provide the mass which is a required value to calculate the spring constant.
The period of oscillation is given by `2pisqrt(m/k)` so the student would need a balance to measure the mass of the object in order to calculate the spring constant.
The photogate would be redundant because the period has already been measured with a stopwatch. It would also neglect to provide the mass which is a required value to calculate the spring constant.

Content: Using a number of measurements, the student determines the following.
problems/AP14P1/media/23a.jpg
The total energy of the object-spring system is most nearly

Key.Rationale: This option is obtained by neglecting to square the velocity in the kinetic energy calculation.
Either the maximum kinetic energy `1/2mv^2` or the maximum spring potential energy `1/2kx^2` can be calculated using the given values and will result in an answer of approximately `4` `text(J)`.
This option is obtained by adding the maximum spring potential and maximum kinetic energy which does not result in the total energy of the system.
This option is obtained by neglecting to square the amplitude in the maximum spring potential energy.

Content: While the object is continuously oscillating, the student determines the maximum speed of the object during `text(two)` oscillations. The `text(first)` speed is `3.5` `text(m)//text(s)` and the `text(second)` speed is `2.7` `text(m)//text(s)` . Which of the following could account for the decrease in the object's maximum kinetic energy?

A.Choice: Energy was transferred from the object to the spring, which increased the maximum potential energy of the spring.

Key.Rationale: Energy transferred to the spring is available to transfer back to the object in the form of kinetic energy. It would not affect the maximum potential energy of the spring or the maximum velocity of the object.

B.Choice: Energy was transferred from the spring to the object, which decreased the maximum potential energy of the spring.

Key.Rationale: Energy transferred to the spring is available to transfer back to the object in the form of kinetic energy. It would not affect the maximum potential energy of the spring or the maximum velocity of the object.

C.Choice: As energy was transferred back and forth between the object and the spring, a greater average share of the energy became potential energy of the spring.

Key.Rationale: Energy transferred to the spring is available to transfer back to the object in the form of kinetic energy. It would not affect the maximum potential energy of the spring or the maximum velocity of the object.

D.Choice: The object-spring system lost energy to its surroundings.

Key.Rationale: For a system's energy to be lost it must be transferred out of the system, not within the system.

Content: How does the new normal force exerted on the crate compare to `F_N`?

A.Choice: The new normal force is greater than `F_N`.

Key.Rationale: If the angle is `text(doubled)`, the vertical component of the applied force is increased. The net vertical force remains `text(zero)` and the gravitational force remains the same, so the normal force must compensate by decreasing.

B.Choice: The new normal force is less than `F_N`.

Key.Rationale: If the angle is `text(doubled)`, the vertical component of the applied force is increased. The net vertical force remains `text(zero)` and the gravitational force remains the same, so the normal force must compensate by decreasing.

C.Choice: The new normal force is equal to `F_N`.

Key.Rationale: If the angle is `text(doubled)`, the vertical component of the applied force is increased. The net vertical force remains `text(zero)` and gravity remains the same, so the normal force cannot remain constant.

D.Choice: The new normal force is greater or less than `F_N` depending on the value of `theta`.

Key.Rationale: As long as the new angle is still between `0°` and `90°`, the new normal force must be less than the original normal force.

Content: As the crate slides a distance `d`, how does the new gain in kinetic energy compare to `DeltaK`?

A.Choice: The new gain is greater than `DeltaK`.

Key.Rationale: An increase in the angle `theta` will result in a decrease in the horizontal component of the applied force. Less work will be done on the crate resulting in a gain in kinetic energy that is less than `DeltaK` because of the Work-Energy Theorem.

B.Choice: The new gain is less than `DeltaK`.

Key.Rationale: An increase in the angle `theta` will result in a decrease in the horizontal component of the applied force. Less work will be done on the crate resulting in a gain in kinetic energy that is less than `DeltaK` because of the Work-Energy Theorem.

C.Choice: The new gain is equal to `DeltaK`.

Key.Rationale: An increase in the angle `theta` will result in a decrease in the horizontal component of the applied force. Less work will be done on the crate resulting in a gain in kinetic energy that is less than `DeltaK` because of the Work-Energy Theorem.

D.Choice: The new gain is greater or less than `DeltaK` depending on the value of `theta`.

Key.Rationale: As long as the new angle is still between `0°` and `90°`, the new gain in kinetic energy must be less than `DeltaK`.

Content: Alan and Beverly are on opposite sides of a large room when Alan says something to Beverly. Beverly does not hear him, so Alan repeats the message louder and Beverly now hears it. Which of the following could be different about the `text(second)` sound wave compared to the `text(first)` that allows Beverly to hear it?

A.Choice: The `text(second)` wave travels to Beverly more quickly, so less energy is dissipated by the time the wave reaches her.

Key.Rationale: Sound travels at a speed based on the conditions of the medium it is traveling through. Increasing the volume increases the amplitude of the sound wave, not the speed.

B.Choice: The `text(second)` wave reflects more off the walls of the room.

Key.Rationale: The material and geometry of the walls aren't changing, so the amount of waves reflected will remain unchanged.

C.Choice: The air molecules disturbed by the `text(second)` wave undergo a greater displacement from their equilibrium positions.

Key.Rationale: Increasing the volume of sound increases the amplitude of the sound wave meaning that the air molecules will undergo a greater displacement from equilibrium.

D.Choice: The air molecules disturbed by the `text(second)` wave are, on average, more closely spaced.

Key.Rationale: Increasing the volume of sound increases the amplitude of the wave and does not affect the average spacing between the molecules.

`text(Two)` strings differing only in length are attached to the same oscillator, as shown in the figure above. Both are fixed at the other end and are under the same tension. The oscillator creates a transverse wave and is adjusted to the lowest frequency that creates a standing wave on the shorter string. Which of the following explains why there will not be a standing wave on the longer string?

A.Choice: The waves travel at slightly different speeds on the `text(two)` strings.

Key.Rationale: The speed of a wave down the string will only be dependent on the tension in the string and the linear density of the string. If both of those are identical for the `text(two)` strings, then the speed of the waves will be the same down `text(each string)`.

B.Choice: An oscillator frequency that results in a standing wave on a string of `text(one)` length cannot result in a standing wave on a string with a different length.

Key.Rationale: It is possible to set a frequency that results in a standing wave on `text(one)` string and a standing wave of a different harmonic on the `text(second)` string if the lengths of the `text(two)` strings have an appropriate ratio.

C.Choice: The amplitude of the wave does not match the boundary conditions for strings of different length at the same time.

Key.Rationale: The amplitude of the wave will not factor into the ability or inability to create a standing wave, it will only impact the height of the resulting wave.

D.Choice: The wavelength associated with the given frequency does not match the boundary conditions set by the length of the longer string.

Key.Rationale: In order to create a standing wave on a string, the length of the string must be of a proper length so that it is `n//2` times the wavelength of the wave created by the oscillator, where n is a positive integer.

Content: `text(Two)` identical carts are free to move along a straight frictionless track. At time `t_1` , cart `X` is moving at `2.0` `text(m)//text(s)` when it collides with and sticks to cart `Y`, which is initially at rest. Which of the following graphs best shows the velocity of cart `X` before and after the collision?

Key.Rationale: Cart `X` will not continue on with the same velocity after colliding with cart `Y`. This would violate the conservation of momentum. When cart `Y` begins to move it gains momentum and so cart `X` must lose momentum.

Both carts have the same mass and velocity after sticking together, so they have the same momentum requiring them to each have `text(half)` the initial momentum of Cart `X`. The only way for Cart `X` to have more than `text(half)` the momentum is if Cart `X` is more massive than Cart `Y`, which is not the case.

Using conservation of momentum, the final velocity of `1` `text(m)//text(s)`. Cart `Y` will gain `text(half)` of the original momentum and cart `X` will lose `text(half)` of its original momentum resulting in `text(half)` the original velocity for cart `X`.

Colliding with cart `Y` will not cause cart `X` to come to a complete stop. This would be the case if the collision was elastic, but the carts stick together after colliding as the result of a completely inelastic collision.

The pod is launched, and afterward the pod is moving to the right with speed `v_p` and the spaceship is moving to the right with speed `v_f`, where `v_f>v`, as shown in the bottom figure. Which of the following is true of the speed `v_c` of the center of mass of the system after the pod is launched?

Key.Rationale: Because the spaceship is moving with speed `v_f` and the pod has a lower speed, the speed of the center of mass of the system must be somewhere between `v_p` and `v_f`.

There are no external forces acting on the system during the separation, so there is no impulse on the system and no change in the velocity of the center of mass. Because the speed of the center of mass was `v` before the separation, it cannot be greater than `v` after separation.

There are no external forces acting on the system during the separation, so there is no impulse on the system and no change in the velocity of the center of mass. Because the speed of the center of mass was `v` before the separation, it cannot be less than `v` after separation.

Because there are no external forces acting on the system consisting of both the pod and the spaceship, there is no impulse on this system and therefore no change in the velocity of its center of mass. Content: problems/AP14P1/media/34a.jpg

The diagram above shows a top view of a child of mass `M` on a circular platform of mass `5M` that is rotating counterclockwise. Assume the platform rotates without friction. Which of the following describes an action by the child that will result in an increase in the total angular momentum of the child-platform system?

A.Choice: The child moves toward the center of the platform.

Key.Rationale: This action will decrease the angular momentum of the child and increase the angular momentum of the platform. However, there are no external forces on the child-platform system, so the angular momentum of the system does not change.

B.Choice: The child moves away from the center of the platform.

Key.Rationale: This action will increase the angular momentum of the child and decrease the angular momentum of the platform. However, there are no external forces on the child-platform system, so the angular momentum of the system does not change.

C.Choice: The child moves along a circle concentric with the platform (dashed line shown) opposite the direction of the platform's rotation.

Key.Rationale: If the child moves along the circle, the interaction forces between the child and the platform will act to increase the angular momentum of the platform and decrease the angular momentum of the child. However, there are no external forces on the child-platform system, so the angular momentum of the system does not change.

D.Choice: None of the actions described will change the total angular momentum of the child-platform system.

Key.Rationale: All of the actions described result in interaction forces between the child and the platform, but do not result in external torques on the child-platform system. Because there are no external torques on the child-platform system, the angular momentum of the system does not change.

A train is traveling east with constant speed `v_t`. `text(Two)` identical spheres are rolling on the floor of `text(one)` train car. In the frame of reference of the train, the spheres are moving directly toward each other at `text(one)` instant with the same speed `v_p` parallel to the train's motion, as shown in the figure above. What is the velocity of the center of mass of the spheres in the frame of reference of the train and in the frame of reference of a person standing at rest alongside the train?

Key.Rationale: Because the velocity of the center of mass of the spheres is `text(zero)` in the reference frame of the train, it cannot also be `text(zero)` in the reference frame of the person at rest alongside the train.

The spheres are identical and are traveling at the same speed in opposite directions in the reference frame of the train, so the center of mass of the spheres has `text(zero)` velocity in that reference frame. Because the train has velocity `v_t` east in the reference frame of the person alongside the train, and the center of mass of the spheres is at rest in the reference from of the train, the center of mass will also have a velocity `v_t` east in the reference frame of the person alongside the train.
Because the train has speed `v_t` with respect to the person alongside the train, the velocity of the center of mass as measured in the `text(two)` reference frames must differ by `v_t`.

In the reference frame of the person alongside the train `text(one)` sphere has velocity `v_p+v_t` east and `text(one)` sphere has velocity `v_p-v_t` east. For `text(nonzero)` `v_t` the velocity of the center of mass in this reference frame cannot be `text(zero)`.

Content: A satellite that is a spinning cylinder has initial rotational inertia `I_0` and angular velocity `omega_0`. Solar panels unfold from the satellite and are extended outward. The satellite then has rotational inertia `I_f=aI_0` and angular velocity `w_f=bw_0`, where `a` and `b` are constants. Which of the following is true about the constants `a` and `b`?

Key.Rationale: The rotational inertia of an object depends on the distribution of mass within the object. When the panels unfold some of the mass of the satellite moves away from the axis of rotation and the moment of inertia changes, so a cannot equal `1`. This also causes a change in angular velocity, so `b` cannot equal `1`.

When the panels unfold, some of the mass of the satellite is moving away from the axis of rotation, causing the moment of inertia of the satellite to increase, so `a>1`. Because there is no external torque acting on the satellite, angular momentum of the satellite must stay the same at `I_0omega_0=I_fomega_f`. When the moment of inertia increases the angular velocity must decrease, so `b<1`.

Because the moment of inertia of the panels increases, the constant `a` is greater than `text(one)`. Because there is no external torque on the satellite as the panels unfold there can be no change in the angular momentum, and an increase in moment of inertia must coincide with a corresponding decrease in angular velocity, so `b` cannot be equal to `1`.

If both `a` and `b` are less than `text(one)`, then as the panels unfold there is decrease in both moment of inertia and angular velocity of the satellite, and the angular momentum of the satellite would decrease. However, in the absence of a net external torque the angular momentum of the satellite must remain the same.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/37a.jpg

When the circuit shown above is set up, the potential difference across the battery is `3.0` `text(V)`. By how much will the magnitude of the potential difference across `R_2` change when `R_3` is removed and its branch is left open?

A.Choice: The magnitude of the potential difference across `R_2` does not change.

Key.Rationale: When `R_3` is removed, the current in `R_2` changes, therefore the potential difference across `R_2` must change as well.

B.Choice: The magnitude of the potential difference across `R_2` decreases by `0.5` `text(V)`.

Key.Rationale: When `R_3` is removed, the resistance of the circuit increases, and the current in the battery (and in `R_1`) decreases. Because the current in `R_1` decreases, the voltage across it does as well, and (using Kirchhoff's loop rule) the voltage across `R_2` increases.

C.Choice: The magnitude of the potential difference across `R_2` increases by `0.5` `text(V)`.

Key.Rationale: With `R_3` in place, the current in `R_1` splits evenly at the junction above `R_2` and `R_3`, because `R_2` and `R_3` have the same resistance, and the current in `R_2` will be `text(one-half)` of the current in `R_1`. Because `R_1` and `R_2` have the same resistance, the voltage across `R_2` will be `text(one-half)` of the voltage across `R_1`. With `R_3` removed, `R_1` and `R_2` are in series and will have the same current, and because they have the same resistance they will also have the same voltage. From Kirchhoff 's loop rule, the sum of the voltages across `R_1` and `R_2` must equal the battery voltage, so with `R_3` in place the voltage across `R_2` is `1` `text(V)` (and the voltage across `R_1` is `text(double)` that, `2` `text(V)`), and with `R_3` removed, the voltage across `R_2` is `1.5` `text(V)`, the same as `R_1`. The potential difference across `R_2` increases `0.5` `text(V)` from `1` `text(V)` to `1.5` `text(V)`.

D.Choice: The magnitude of the potential difference across `R_2` increases by `1.0` `text(V)`.

Key.Rationale: The potential difference across `R_3` increases by `0.5` `text(V)` as described in the explanation for the correct option.

Content: How does the magnitude of the force exerted by the top box on the bottom box compare with the magnitude of the force exerted by the bottom box on the top box for each of the stacks?

A.Choice: The `text(two)` magnitudes are always equal in each of the stacks.

Key.Rationale: For `text(each stack)` of blocks, the forces being compared form a Newton's `text(third)` law pair (an action-reaction pair) and are therefore equal in magnitude in `text(each case)`.

B.Choice: The `text(two)` magnitudes are always different in each of the stacks.

Key.Rationale: The forces being compared form a Newton's `text(third)` law pair for `text(each stack)` of blocks, and must always have the same magnitude.

C.Choice: The `text(two)` magnitudes are equal when the boxes have equal mass and different when the boxes have different masses.

Key.Rationale: The forces being compared form a Newton's `text(third)` law pair for `text(each stack)` of blocks, and must always have the same magnitude. These forces are normal forces, not gravitational forces.

D.Choice: The `text(two)` magnitudes are equal when the elevator is moving at constant speed and different when it is accelerating.

Key.Rationale: The forces being compared form a Newton's `text(third)` law pair for `text(each stack)` of blocks, and Newton's `text(third)` law is valid whether the objects in question are accelerating or not.

Content: Assume the elevator is moving at constant speed, and consider the bottom box in the stack that has `text(two)` boxes of mass `2M`. Let `F_text(floor)` be the force exerted by the floor on the box, `F_g` be the force exerted by gravity on the box, and `F_text(box)` be the force exerted by the top box on the bottom box. Which of the following best represents the forces exerted on the bottom box?

Key.Rationale: There is a downward normal force exerted on the bottom box by the top box.
There is a downward gravitational force on the bottom box by the `text(Earth)`.

The gravitational force on the blocks must be the same, because they have the same mass. Both boxes are moving upward with constant velocity, so the net force on `text(each box)` must be `text(zero)`. The only forces acting on the top box are the upward normal force by the bottom box and the gravitation force, so the normal force must have the same magnitude as the gravitation force. The normal force downward on the bottom box must be equal in magnitude to the upward normal force on the top box (they form a Newton's `text(third)` law pair). So the gravitational force on the bottom box by the `text(Earth)` must have the same magnitude as the normal force on the bottom box by the top box (both of these point downward). Because the net force on the bottom box is `text(zero)` the `text(two)` downward forces must balance the upward force by
The force exerted by the top box on the bottom box is a downward normal force.

Content: Assume the elevator has upward acceleration `a`, and consider the stack that has `text(two)` boxes of mass `M`. What is the magnitude of the force exerted on the top box by the bottom box?

Key.Rationale: The upward force exerted on the top box by the bottom box must be greater than the downward gravitational force on the top box (`Mg`) because the top box is accelerating upward.

In addition to the upward force exerted on the top box by is a downward gravitational force on the top box. In order for the net force on the top box to be equal to `Ma`, the upward force by the bottom box must be greater than `Ma`.

If the top box were moving upward with no acceleration, there would be no net force acting on it, so the upward force exerted on the top box by the bottom box would be equal to the downward gravitational force `Mg`. The upward force must be greater than this to obtain an upward acceleration, so `a` and `g` must add together as described in the explanation for the correct option.

The forces acting on the top box are the downward gravitational force by the `text(Earth)` (`Mg`) and an upward normal force on the top box by the bottom box `F_N`. Because the top box is accelerating upward, there must be a net upward force on it equal to `Ma`. From Newton's `text(second)` law we have `F_N-MG=Ma`, so `F_N=M(a+g)`.

Content: A researcher is analyzing data from a high-energy particle collision. The result of the analysis gives a value of `8.8xx10^-19` `text(C)+-0.1xx10^-19` `text(C)` for the charge of `text(one)` of the emitted particles. Should the researcher accept the value?

A.Choice: Yes, it is a perfectly acceptable value.

Key.Rationale: A particle emitted from a collision will have a charge that is an integer multiple of the elementary charge `1.6xx10^-19` `text(C)`. `text(Five)` times the elementary charge is `8.8xx10^-19` `text(C)`, and `text(six)` times the elementary charge is `9.6xx10^-19` `text(C)`. The analysis gives a value for a charge from `8.7xx10^-19` `text(C)` to `8.9xx10^-19` `text(C)`, which is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

B.Choice: No, because the value is much bigger than the elementary charge.

Key.Rationale: The relative size is not the crucial consideration, as long as the value obtained is an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

C.Choice: No, because the value is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

Key.Rationale: A particle emitted from a collision will have a charge that is an integer multiple of the elementary charge `1.6xx10^-19` `text(C)`. `text(Five)` times the elementary charge is `8.0xx10^-19` `text(C)`, and `text(six)` times the elementary charge is `9.6xx10^-19` `text(C)`. The analysis gives a range of values between `8.7xx10^-19` `text(C)` and `8.9xx10^-19` `text(C)`, which is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

D.Choice: No, because the uncertainty is more than `1%` of the value.

Key.Rationale: There are many useful experiments with an uncertainty greater than `1%` of the value to be determined.

Content: A student wants to determine the speed of sound at an elevation of `text(one mile)`. To do this the student performs an experiment to determine the resonance frequencies of a tube that is closed at `text(one)` end. The student takes measurements `text(every day)` for a `text(week)` and gets different results on different `text(days)`. Which of the following experiments would help the student determine the reason for the different results?

A.Choice: Repeating the experiment on several `10°text(C)` `text(days)` and several `20°text(C)` `text(days)`

Key.Rationale: Temperature is an uncontrolled variable in the original experiment, and the modification described helps both to learn whether the frequencies change when temperature changes, and to see whether frequencies stay the same when temperature is constant.

B.Choice: Repeating the experiment using a longer tube

Key.Rationale: The length of the tube was not varied in the original experiment, and yet the frequencies changed. The tube length did not cause the variation.

C.Choice: Repeating the experiment using a wider range of frequencies of sound

Key.Rationale: With a wider range of frequencies and equivalent conditions, the same variation of results would be expected for frequencies that were in the original experiment.

D.Choice: Repeating the original experiment for an additional `text(week)`

Key.Rationale: The same variation of results would be expected with a longer experiment.

Content: Some students have determined the gravitational mass of an object and want to compare it to the object's inertial mass. Procedures that would allow them to accomplish this include which of the following? Select `text(two)` answers.

A.Choice: Hanging the object vertically from a spring scale and recording the scale reading

Key.Rationale: The process of hanging the object vertically on a spring scale determines only the weight of the object or gravitational mass but does not compare to inertial mass. The procedure relies upon the gravitational field.

B.Choice: Placing the object on `text(one)` side of a `text(double)` pan balance, adding objects of known mass to the other side until the masses are balanced, and recording the amount of mass added

Key.Rationale: The process described here compares the effect of gravity on both sides of a pan balance, so only gravitational mass is considered. There is no comparison to inertial mass. This procedure relies upon the gravitational field.

C.Choice: Attaching the object to a spring of known spring constant, allowing it to oscillate horizontally on a nearly frictionless surface, and measuring the period

Key.Rationale: For the spring oscillating horizontally, measuring the period (with a known spring constant) allows students to calculate the inertial mass of the object attached to the spring. This can now be compared to the gravitational mass determined previously. This procedure would work without a gravitational field.

D.Choice: Attaching the object to a force sensor, using the sensor to pull the object across a nearly frictionless horizontal surface, and measuring the acceleration

Key.Rationale: Pulling the object across a horizontal surface allows application of Newton's `text(second)` law in the horizontal direction, which determines the inertial mass (knowing the force and acceleration). This procedure would work without a gravitational field.

The figure above shows a representation of a wave traveling in a uniform medium at a particular instant. Correct statements about the wave include which of the following? Select `text(two)` answers.

Key.Rationale: At the instant shown, the particles in the medium have been displaced from their equilibrium positions along the direction of travel of the wave, so the wave is a longitudinal wave.
The wave pattern repeats itself from any point along the wave to a `text(second)` point a distance `a` away. Distance `a` is therefore the wavelength of the wave.

C.Choice: The number of dots `text(per unit length)` is the frequency.

Key.Rationale: The frequency of the wave is the number of times a `text(single)` particle repeats its periodic motion `text(per unit time)`.

D.Choice: The largest distance between `text(two)` successive dots is the amplitude.

Key.Rationale: The amplitude of the wave is the maximum displacement of a `text(single)` particle from its rest position.

Content: problems/AP14P1/media/50a.jpg

A geologist is using a sensor to record waves in a layer of rock and is viewing them on a monitor screen. At `text(one)` moment the monitor shows the signal above. If the signal is created by just `text(two)` traveling waves, what can be concluded from the signal about the waves when they reach the sensor? Select `text(two)` answers.

Key.Rationale: The pattern shown is a beat pattern created by the superposition of `text(two)` waves of slightly different frequencies. The amplitude of the wave varies as a function of time because at the position of the sensor the `text(two)` waves sometimes constructively interfere and sometimes destructively interfere.

When the `text(two)` waves destructively interfere, the amplitude of the superposition of the waves is at a minimum. If the `text(two)` traveling waves had the same amplitude, the destructive interference would give a resultant `text(zero)` amplitude wave at the minimum. The wave on the monitor has a `text(nonzero)` minimum.

C.Choice: The waves are traveling in opposite directions.

Key.Rationale: The direction of motion of the individual waves cannot be determined from either the signal measured at a `text(single)` location or an instantaneous view of the signal.

D.Choice: The waves are traveling at different speeds.

Key.Rationale: Both traveling waves are traveling to the sensor through the same layer of rock, and because they are in the same medium, they have the same speed.
